name: Gungnir
powers: Never misses its mark; its throwers and possession pledge a solemn oath.
description: The spear of Odin, forged by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi in a contest against Brokkr and Sindri for Loki's head. The All-Father opened the war between the Æsir and Vanir by hurling Gungnir over the enemy host, an act that became the archetype of casting a spear at the start of a battle. Oaths sworn upon it were considered unbreakable. Odin rides with it at Ragnarök.

name: Gleipnir
powers: Unbreakable binding that holds the wolf Fenrir until Ragnarök.
description: The third and final fetter with which the gods bound the wolf Fenrir, after the chains Lœdingr and Drómi snapped. Forged by the dwarves from six impossible things: the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, and a bird's spittle. Made as thin as silk, it cannot be broken. The god Týr placed his hand in Fenrir's mouth as a pledge and lost it when the wolf discovered he could not free himself.

name: Gram
maker: Reforged by Regin from the shards of Sigmund's blade
powers: Slices through a smith's anvil and the body of the dragon Fáfnir.
description: The sword of the Völsung heroes. Its first owner Sigmund drove it into the Branstock tree, where none but he could pull it out. When the blade broke, the shards were kept and reforged by Regin for Sigmund's son Sigurðr, who proved the blade by splitting the anvil in two and later used it to slay the dragon Fáfnir.

name: Gjallarhorn
powers: Its sound carries across all the worlds; it calls the gods to the final battle.
description: The great horn of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods, who guards the rainbow bridge Bifröst. In the Prose Edda, Heimdallr drinks from it at the well and will blow it when the world ends; at Ragnarök the horn's blast is heard throughout the worlds, summoning gods and men to the final battle. It may double as a drinking vessel in some accounts.

name: Gallehus Golden Horns
maker: Maker named in runic inscription: LagestheR
powers: Ceremonial drinking and ritual horns; images thought to invoke protection and fertility.
description: Two golden horns of the 5th century, found at Gallehus in southern Jutland in 1639 and 1734 and stolen and melted down in 1802. The longer horn bore a runic inscription naming its maker, LagestheR. The horns' densely decorated bands of men, beasts, and symbols have been read as ritual or cultic imagery. Reconstructions are held in Copenhagen; they remain among the most famous objects of Nordic antiquity.

name: Gullinbursti
powers: Its golden bristles light the darkest night, and it runs through air and water faster than any horse.
description: Freyr's golden boar, forged by the dwarves Brokkr and Sindri during the same wager that produced Mjölnir. Its bristles shone so brightly that they lit the dark, and it could run through air and water alike. Odin judged it the finest of the dwarves' treasures, and Snorri records it as fit to draw Freyr's chariot in place of a horse.

name: Gríðarvölr
powers: A staff of might lent to Thor, with which he slew the giant Geirröðr.
description: The staff of the giantess Gríðr, lent by her to Thor along with iron gloves and a belt of might when he set out against the giant Geirröðr. With the staff in hand Thor broke Geirröðr's back and killed him. The loan, told in Skáldskaparmál, is a rare act of kindness by a giantess toward the thunder god.

name: Ginfaxi
powers: Turns the luck of a rival or competitor, so the bearer wins the contest.
description: Ginfaxi, the rival-beating stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn to defeat an opponent in competition or argument. Its name echoes the animal names of Norse myth, but here it belongs to a sign meant to turn luck against rivals. It is one of the combative staves of Icelandic folk magic, used when the prize was trade, a case, or a contest.

name: Galdrastafir
material: Inscribed wood, drawn on paper and skin
powers: A family of sigils drawn for protection, luck, healing, or harm, each with a specific aim.
description: Galdrastafir, the collective name for the magical staves of Icelandic folk tradition, drawn from the 17th century onward in grimoires such as the Huld manuscript. Each stave mixes rune-like strokes into a sigil for a single aim — protection, luck, healing, or harm. They form the best-documented stave-magic corpus in Europe, though many survive without clear instructions for use.

name: Iðunn's Golden Apples
powers: Keep the gods from ageing; without them the gods grey and weaken.
description: The golden apples of Iðunn, which the gods must eat to keep from growing old. When the giant Þjazi tricked Loki into luring Iðunn out of Asgard, the gods aged and greyed, until Loki stole her back in falcon shape, carrying her and her apples from the giant's stronghold. The apples are a life-giving treasure whose loss threatens the whole pantheon.

name: Grotte Mill
maker: Unnamed; turned by the giantesses Fenja and Menja
powers: Grinds out gold, peace, and abundance for its owner; overgrinds to catastrophe.
description: The great hand-mill owned by King Fróði, which ground out gold, peace, and abundance. In the Eddic poem Grottasöngr the giantesses Fenja and Menja were forced to turn it until they raised an army; carried aboard a ship, the mill then ground salt until it sank, and so the sea became salt. The same wonder-mill lies at the heart of the Swedish folktale 'Why the Sea Is Salt'.
source: Grottasöngr (Poetic Edda); Swedish folktale 'Why the Sea Is Salt'

name: The Golden Keys
powers: Unlock doors and rewards for the hero who wins them.
description: Golden keys that appear in a Swedish folk tale, unlocking a reward or a forbidden treasure for the hero who obtains them. The keys belong to the tale's wonder-logic: ordinary locks fall open before them, and possession of the keys brings the hero to fortune. The motif is told as part of the tale 'The Golden Keys'.

name: The Golden Cradle
description: A cradle of gold in a Swedish folk tale, in which a special child is laid and around which the tale's wonder unfolds. In 'The Golden Cradle', the precious cradle marks the child's destiny and the family's fortune, and its making or finding drives the story. The golden cradle is an emblem of the wonder-tale's promise of wealth and favour.

name: Gjermundbu Helmet
description: The only reasonably complete Viking-age helmet found in Scandinavia, recovered from a wealthy chieftain's burial mound at Gjermundbu in Ringerike, Norway, in 1943. The iron helmet has a rounded cap, a spectacle-like eye guard, and a mail curtain for the neck, and was buried with a mail coat, swords, and gaming pieces. It now stands in the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo.

name: Gokstad Ship
description: A seaworthy Viking-age longship found in a burial mound at Gokstad in Sandefjord, Norway, in 1880. Around 23 meters long with sixteen pairs of oars, it was built for open-sea sailing and held the remains of a chieftain. A full-scale copy, the Viking, crossed the Atlantic to Chicago in 1893, proving its sailing qualities. The original is displayed in the Viking Ship Museum in Oslo.

name: Gákti
material: Wool with tin-thread and pewter embroidery
description: The traditional dress of the Sámi, a tunic worn with a decorated collar, belt, and headgear, trimmed with bands of red, blue, and yellow and pewter-thread embroidery. Each region of Sápmi has its own cut, colors, and embroidery, so the dress tells the wearer's origin and family. The gákti is still worn for ceremonies and festivals and carries strong cultural identity among Sámi in Norway.

name: Guksi
description: The Sámi cup carved from a birch burl, with a handle and a shallow bowl, traditionally worn at the belt for coffee, broth, and water. Each guksi is shaped from a single piece of burled birch and seasoned by use, so a worn cup becomes a prized possession among reindeer herders. Carving is a handwork tradition passed down in Sámi families in Norway and Finland.

name: Gjellestad Ship
description: A Viking-age ship burial discovered at Gjellestad in Østfold, Norway, first detected with ground-penetrating radar in 2018 and excavated from 2020. The oak keel and strakes of the roughly 20-meter ship survived in wet clay, along with beads, iron, and a soapstone vessel. It is the first ship burial excavated in Norway in over a century.

name: The Great Cat of Dovrefjell
powers: Its presence terrifies trolls and drives them from the house.
description: The monstrous cat of the Norwegian folktale collected by Asbjørnsen and Moe, in which a traveller brings his cat to a Dovrefjell farm whose Christmas feast is ruined by trolls every year. When the trolls return, the cat seizes the troll wife and is taken for an enormous bear, and the trolls flee. Learning that the great cat still lives, they never come back.

name: Gundestrup Cauldron
description: A richly decorated silver cauldron found dismantled in a peat bog at Gundestrup in Himmerland, Jutland, in 1891. Its plates show gods, warriors, horned figures, and a great cauldron in which a figure is dipped, imagery with links to Celtic and Thracian art. It was probably made abroad and carried north, then offered to the bog as a sacrificial gift. It is kept in the National Museum of Denmark.

name: Golden Fleece
maker: The ram Chrysomallus, sent by Hermes
powers: Object of the quest of the Argonauts; hung in the grove of Ares under a dragon's guard.
description: The golden fleece of the winged ram that carried Phrixus and Helle to Colchis; Jason and the Argonauts sailed to retrieve it from the grove of Ares, where a sleepless dragon guarded it. It is the goal of the Argonaut cycle, the price King Aeetes demanded of Jason before he would surrender it.
source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca

name: Golden Bough
maker: Hidden in the wood of Proserpina
powers: Admitted a living man into the underworld; the offering Proserpina required of Aeneas.
description: The golden bough Aeneas plucked in the Sibyl's wood to gain entry to the underworld and offer to Proserpina; like mistletoe it must be found and plucked by fate alone, and its presence admits the living to the realm of the dead. Virgil makes it the passport of the Aeneid's descent.

name: Portuguese Guitar
material: Wood, metal strings (twelve strings in six courses)
maker: Developed from the English cittern in Lisbon
powers: The signature voice of fado, said to express saudade itself.
description: The Portuguese guitar, a twelve-string cittern with a pear-shaped body, the defining instrument of fado; its bright, plaintive sound accompanies the singer in Lisbon's taverns and is said to voice saudade itself. A documented tradition of urban song rather than a mythic relic, it anchors Portugal's musical folklore.
source: Ethnographic and musicological documentation of the fado tradition

name: Gusle
material: Maple bowl, single horse-hair string, horse-hair bow
powers: Accompanied heroic epic song in the oral tradition of the southern Balkans.
description: The gusle, a single-stringed fiddle of the Balkan epic singers, played with a bow while the singer chants heroic songs; on the Croatian coast and hinterland it accompanied tales of heroes and outlaws, and the instrument is inseparable from the region's oral heroic tradition, documented among Croats, Serbs, and Montenegrins.
source: Ethnographic documentation of the South Slavic epic tradition

name: Ivory Statue of Galatea
powers: Brought to life by Aphrodite at Pygmalion's prayer; became his wife.
description: The ivory statue the sculptor Pygmalion of Cyprus carved and fell in love with; at his prayer Aphrodite brought it to life as Galatea, who became his wife. Ovid's Metamorphoses tells the story, the classic tale of art animated by desire, and it is set on the island of Cyprus.

name: The Green Knight's Axe
powers: Weapon of the beheading challenge at Camelot.
description: The enormous green-steel axe carried by the Green Knight into King Arthur's hall at the start of the fourteenth-century poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. Gawain strikes the Knight's head off with it, and the Knight picks up the severed head, which reminds Gawain of the return blow owed at the Green Chapel.
source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (fourteenth century)

name: Green Knight's Holly Branch
description: The holly branch carried by the Green Knight in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight when he rides unarmed into Arthur's hall. Its evergreen branches mark him as one of the winter gods of the older year, and he uses it to hold his own axe as he delivers his challenge. It is an emblem of the poem's beheading-game and seasonal cycle.
source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

name: The Golden Goose
powers: Stuck fast anyone who touched it, drawing a growing chain of followers.
description: Die goldene Gans, the goose from the Grimms' tale of the same name. Found by Dummling in the wood, the golden goose sticks fast to anyone who touches it, so that the whole town follows in a chain behind him; the sight makes the sad princess laugh, winning her hand. The goose is a purely fictional marvel.

name: The Golden Falcon of Hierakonpolis
powers: The earliest great image of the falcon god Horus.
description: A gold head of the falcon god Horus found in the main deposit of the temple at Hierakonpolis, dated to about 3100 BCE, one of the oldest large cult images of a deity to survive from Egypt. With its obsidian eyes and worked gold feathers, it stood as the focus of worship at the site where the Narmer Palette was also found, marking the beginnings of pharaonic divine kingship.

name: The Grail of Qumran
aliases: Holy Grail of the Dead Sea
powers: None attested; a modern identification without support.
description: A drinking vessel that popular speculation has linked with the Dead Sea Scrolls community at Qumran and identified with the Holy Grail of Christian legend. No manuscript, inscription, or excavation connects any Qumran cup to the Grail tradition, and the identification is a modern theory built on suggestion rather than any primary source. It is a derived claim, not an attested artifact.

name: The Gris-gris
maker: Fqih (learned man) who wrote the contents
powers: Protects, heals, or brings luck by the written words sealed inside.
description: A small leather pouch worn on the body, holding written Qur'anic verses, prayers, or magic squares, used across North Africa to protect, heal, or bring fortune. In Morocco the hirz was stitched by a fqih and worn at the neck or arm, its power resting entirely on the writing sealed inside. The custom is documented in ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk practice and survives today.
source: Ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk practice

name: Guan Dao
material: Steel blade on a long wooden shaft
powers: Emblem of martial protection and the god of war
description: The heavy curved-blade polearm historically carried by Guan Yu, the Three Kingdoms general deified as the god of war. The 'Green Dragon Crescent Blade' is the most famous of its kind; ceremonial guan dao are still kept in martial temples and used in lion-dance and martial-arts displays to invoke his protection.

name: Geobukseon
powers: Iron-roofed warship that shed fire and boarding parties
description: The armored turtle warship built for Admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet in the 1590s, roofed with an iron-studded shell that shed flame and repelled boarders. Though a real historical vessel, it passed into Korean folklore as an invincible protector of the coast, celebrated in songs and tales of the Imjin War against the Japanese invasion.

name: Gogok
powers: Symbol of rank, fertility, and the sun
description: The comma-shaped jade ornament threaded onto the gold crowns and belts of the Silla kingdom and excavated in numbers from the tombs of Gyeongju. Scholars link the curved bead to the bear-woman Ungnyeo's offering in the Dangun myth and to shamanic fertility symbolism; it remains the emblem of ancient Korean royal regalia.

name: The Golden Whip of Genghis Khan
powers: Said to rally and reward warriors of the khan
description: The golden whip that legend says Genghis Khan carried, brandished to rally and reward his warriors, and in some tellings the source of his military genius. No such whip survives or is named in the Secret History; the story is a modern heroic retelling of the conqueror's rise rather than a documented relic.

name: Gris-Gris Bag
material: Red flannel pouch with herbs, roots, coins or stones
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Carries the working of the root doctor for love, luck or protection.
description: A small flannel pouch filled with herbs, roots, stones or personal items, made by Louisiana root doctors and hoodoo practitioners to carry a working for love, luck, money or protection; gris-gris is the name used in New Orleans, mojo in other regions. The practice blends African spiritual traditions with colonial folk belief. Bags are carried on the body and often must be fed to take effect.
source: Louisiana hoodoo tradition and ethnographic records

name: Govi
era: Haitian Vodou tradition to the present
powers: Holds the spirits of the ancestors and the dead.
description: A clay jar or bottle used in Haitian Vodou to contain the presence of the dead or the spirits of the ancestors, kept in the temple and opened with care by the priest. The govi is an ordinary vessel made extraordinary by the ritual that fills it, and its handling is governed by strict rules of respect. It links the community of the living with the world beneath.
source: Haitian Vodou practice and ethnographic studies
